sections.title: One rule sorts them all
sections.content: You know *es posible que* and *dudo que* with the subjunctive, and *es evidente que* with the indicative, from B1 Unit 13, and *no creo que* from B1 Unit 7. Spanish has a whole family of expressions like these, and one rule sorts them. If you present something as certain, use the indicative. If you only say that it is probable, possible or doubtful, use the subjunctive. Saying that a certain thing is *not* certain also takes the subjunctive.

sections.title: Three groups
rows: You present it as a fact, so: indicative. Also está claro que, es seguro que, no hay duda de que.
You only say how likely it is, so: subjunctive. Also es posible que, es poco probable que, es improbable que.
You say that a certain thing is not certain, so: subjunctive. Also no está claro que, no es evidente que.

sections.title: Things that already happened
sections.content: For a past event, use the present perfect subjunctive from B1 Unit 37 after the expressions of the second and third group: *Es probable que hayan salido*, *No es seguro que lo haya visto*.

items.spanish: Es evidente que Marta sabe la verdad.
items.english: It is clear that Marta knows the truth.

items.spanish: Es probable que Marta sepa la verdad.
items.english: It is probable that Marta knows the truth.

items.spanish: No es seguro que Marta sepa la verdad.
items.english: It is not certain that Marta knows the truth.

items.spanish: No hay duda de que Marta sabe la verdad.
items.english: There is no doubt that Marta knows the truth.

items.spanish: Es poco probable que hayan salido tan temprano.
items.english: It is unlikely that they left so early.

sections.content: Watch the negatives that are not negative. *No hay duda de que* and *no dudo que* mean that you are sure, so they take the indicative, while *dudo que* and *es dudoso que* take the subjunctive. The question to ask is always: am I presenting this as certain?
